>SHOOT THE PIRATE
Trembling, you fire the heavy arquebus. You hear its loud report over the
roaring wind, yet the dark figure still approaches. The gun falls from your
nerveless hands.
   "You won't kill me," he says, stepping over the weapon. "Not when I am
the only protection you have from Jean Lafond."
   Chestnut hair, tousled by the wind, frames the tanned oval of his face.
Lips curving, his eyes rake over your inadequately dressed body, the damp
chemise clinging to your legs and heaving bosom, your gleaming hair. You
are intensely aware of the strength of his hard seaworn body, of the deep
sea blue of his eyes. And then his mouth is on yours, lips parted,
demanding, and you arch into his kiss...
   He presses you against him, head bent. "But who, my dear," he whispers
into your hair, "will protect you from me?"

match_full.title: Balancing Reality and Fiction in Games
match_full.excerpt: Um earlier I wanted to say when when asking about Steve giving advice, he may not have needed to give advice because I had read him in a at the time I was working there. I read his an interview with him. I think it was may have been for Games Magazine that that struck me at the time and and I still obviously remember it today which is he said there's this fine line with with reality and with setting up how the games how the rooms are described. He said, "If you if you say you walk into an office, there's a desk there. The player is going to expect the whole world of things that are on a typical desk, a stapler, a phone, you know, a pencil cup. Who knows what they're going to expect?" And you don't want to waste your time as a as an implementer coding in every single possible thing that could possibly be on a desktop when what you really only care about is, you know, the magic pen that's in the pencil cup. Um, whereas if you say you walk into a wizard's uh lab or a wizard's cave, who knows what's in a wizard's cave. So you can get away with a lot by setting it in this fantasy at environment that people don't have predetermined expectations about what should be in that environment. Um, and and so I think that's some of what you're talking about of of at the level of the ters's job was not just to find bugs. the rather dull QA of where does the computer crash. It's where does the world that you've invented break down and what is a reasonable approximation of things that are on the desk. Let's say that people will look for without having to burden the code with everything possible. And you could argue that in Plundered Hearts I didn't I didn't broaden it enough. I didn't get enough of those because people were complaining you can't karate chop or or things. Um, certainly I know I'm still embarrassed to this day in the final released version there's a bug that happens in the first couple moves, when you do something very logical and I can't remember what it is right now but it then that's a it's a true bug. You get garbage if you type out something like take the box there's a box under the bed that slides out and if you take the box rather than grab the box or something that's a logical thing to do you get garbage from it. So that was a case where the testers had missed or I missed in in my own I should take responsibility a very obvious thing to have done at the beginning.

match_full.title: Creating a Romance Game for Women
match_full.excerpt: That was I will take the credit and the blame. I think that was all my idea. I mean, I think they were fine with me going forward with it. And it wasn't that there hadn't been women writing text adventures before. Um, even in our company, though they hadn't been, you know, the main imp. Um, but I think it was a good selling point of, oh, look, and there was this movement at that time. is before Brenda Laurel and before I think it's Purple Moon, which has gone out of business now, but the games for girls, the games that they were coming out for girls at that time were like cooking games. Oh, let's have a sewing game and which is just benited. It it just the concept that and they weren't fun to play either. Um so, no wonder girls weren't interested in playing them. I'm not actually going to claim that Plundered Hearts is a game that girls would be that interested in playing because I think the mode of play is something that developmentally teenage girls aren't that interested in doing sitting down with a computer by yourself. I think Brenda Laurel and some other companies have done good ways of of getting games that girls will be interested in playing. But we didn't know that then. And I was interested in in writing romance. I thought a romance might be kind of fun and different. And it had this, you know, this gimmick of a woman writing for women. So there were at the time there were some critical reviews that just hated it because of its over femininess. And I remember one reviewer just lit into the game because she was trying to karate chop and to do tough guy stuff and the game wouldn't let her. And so she was criticizing it for not allowing uh the character to be strong. And we can go into a whole sort of philosophical approach about what a character should be in one of these games.

match_full.title: A Young Company of Passionate Developers
match_full.excerpt: So the other side of it was again from my experience from within the whole company we were all very young. I was younger than the average, but I was like 22, 23. Um, but but and the guys, somebody can tell you what the average age, there's a t-shirt that was given to the first person who would age, the oldest person in the company, you know. I' get into work to test, you know, at 9:00, 9:30, 10:00. I'd work till 6:30 or 7:00 and then I'd work on the game for 2 or 3 hours. Go out to dinner with somebody, you know, else who was working late, come back. The company was open and there all the time. It was just part of the whole culture of the company. I was not alone in this is what I mean to say. You'd see other people there at the company, not writing their own games necessarily, but there to play games on the computers that we had available or to just hang out, everything. So, I guess in that way, it was probably different from other places I've worked.

   A crash overhead! Pirates are boarding the Lafond Deux! The first mate
hurries you into Captain Davis's cabin.
   "Good, you brought the girl," Davis smirks. "She'll keep the pirates
busy. She was only a tool of Lafond's, anyway. Let me just find that cof--"
A man on deck screams in agony and Davis starts. "Let's go." The captain
thrusts you on the bed and walks out, locking the door.
   His laugh echoes. "Best get comfortable, girl. You're likely to be there
for the rest of your life."

Cabin, on the bed

porthole. A door is to starboard. Except for the built-in bed, the room
seems to have been emptied thoroughly, if hurriedly.
